Day 66 of 100 · Docker

Docker Networks

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityDockerPublished artifact recovered

User-defined Docker networks let containers discover one another by names or aliases instead of coupling applications to replaceable container IP addresses.

Architecture / mental model

app container → user-defined bridge DNS → db container
external client → published host port → app container

How it works

On a single Docker host, a user-defined bridge network provides an isolated L2/L3 network and Docker-managed name resolution for attached containers.

The published lab created `app-net`, started a database named `db` and an application named `app` on that network. The application could reach the database at `db:5432` without knowing the database container's current IP.

Port publishing solves a different problem. `-p 8080:8000` exposes the application's container port through the host; the database does not need a public host port merely because the application needs to reach it internally.

Hands-on reference

docker network ls
docker network create app-net
docker run -d --name db --network app-net -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=demo-only postgres:17-alpine
docker run -d --name app --network app-net -p 8080:8000 myapp:1.0
docker network inspect app-net

Verification

Recreate the database container on the same user-defined network and confirm the application can continue using the `db` name rather than a hard-coded IP. Inspect network membership and DNS behavior.

Field note / gotcha

Automatic container-name DNS is a feature of user-defined networks; do not assume every Docker network mode has identical service-discovery behavior.

Security considerations

Do not publish internal services to the host unless external access is required. Network segmentation reduces accidental reachability but is not an authentication system.

What I learned

Names and aliases are application dependencies; ephemeral container IPs are implementation details.
